paras: The attempted lynching of James Curby happened at Versailles, Kentucky, on Wednesday, November 7, 1888, when a mob of Black residents chased and captured Curby, a Black man accused of raping a six-year-old girl. Town authorities took him from the mob and jailed him, and the dispatch reported threats to storm the jail.

According to a dispatch from Versailles dated November 9, Curby was accused of assaulting the six-year-old daughter of Silas Mitchell, whom the dispatch also described as "colored." After the alleged assault, Curby fled the town, and what the dispatch called "an infuriated mob of colored citizens" followed and caught him. The mob "would have lynched him," the report said, if the town authorities had not stepped in, arrested him and lodged him in jail.

Even with Curby in jail, "the colored people made threats of mobbing the jail," the dispatch said, and it reported that the child was "not seriously injured." The coverage contains no report of an indictment, a trial, or any action against members of the mob.

On November 9 the Maysville Evening Bulletin in Kentucky and the Clarksville Evening Chronicle in Tennessee printed the same short wire item, word for word, under the headline "Criminal Saved By Officers." The item called the alleged crime "a dastardly outrage" and Curby "a burly colored ruffian," stating the accusation as fact while giving the authorities credit for preventing a lynching. The dispatch identified the accused, the girl's father and the mob all as "colored," and it gave the mob's pursuit no comment beyond noting that the town authorities had interfered.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of James Curby
bases: A mob pursued and captured a man accused of rape and 'would have lynched him' had town authorities not jailed him, then threatened to mob the jail (A1, A2).

The dispatch describes a mob that captured Curby on a rape accusation and intended to lynch him, but town authorities took him from it and jailed him, and no killing is reported (A1, A2); it was an attempted lynching.
Both reports are the same wire dispatch, word for word, so the account rests on one source (A1, A2).
